stops.note: from mel 'honey'; with no cane sugar, Romans sweetened with honey and defrutum, grape must boiled down to a syrup
Portugal's sugar plantations on Madeira, producing by the mid-1400s, left this dark syrup as the by-product of boiling cane juice; the industry then moved to São Tomé and Brazil
spelled 'melasses' at first; it became a pillar of the Atlantic triangular trade, distilled into New England rum and taxed by Britain's Molasses Act of 1733
stops.meaning: thick dark syrup from sugar cane

current_meaning: thick dark syrup left over from refining sugar
